title: Hosting econ qualification - Pecan Finance
next_steps: Redwood to send pilot pricing sheet and per-token forecast (Maya)
Customer to share 1-week sample traffic trace and example prompts (Lena)
Schedule 60m technical pilot kickoff with SE and infra (Diego + Samir)
action_items: Maya: email pilot pricing and benchmark template by 2026-08-24
Lena: upload obfuscated 7-day query sample to shared drive by 2026-08-25
Diego: prepare suggested batching and cache config for initial pilot (no later than 2026-08-27)
summary: Initial qualification focusing on per-token economics, tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC, and pilot scope constrained by a $12k monthly inference budget. Customer prioritized 100ms P99 latency for auth flows and wants a three-week pilot that demonstrates ~30% cost reduction via batching/caching.
topics: per-token pricing and target unit economics
hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Maya from Redwood. well kick off with quick intros.
[00:05] Lena Ortiz: hi i'm lena, head of ml at pecan finance. we run fraud detection and consent flows where latency matters.
[00:10] Samir Patel: samir, eng mgr, looking at integration and cost buckets.
[00:15] Renee Cho: renee, security architect, paging through compliance questions.
[00:20] Tom Briggs: tom, product, curious about UX impact.
[00:25] Marcus: (audio) hey, finance - running numbers in background.
[00:28] Maya Chen: cool, quick agenda: baseline current infra, cost targets, discuss levers (batching, kv cache, quant), map hosting options (hosted/dedicated/private), and agree pilot next steps. Diego from our SE team will jump to technicals after the budget stuff.
[00:40] Tom Briggs: sounds good.
[00:44] Lena Ortiz: i'll start. our immediate use-case is enrichments on auth flows: we augment login signals with an LLM-based risk summary. about 100k requests/day now, average prompt ~150 tokens in, 60 tokens out. We want P99 latency around 100-150ms because it sits inline with our login path. We got a 12k/mo budget for inference that we can't easily exceed this fiscal quarter.
[01:10] Samir Patel: and we' re evaluating whether to use a hosted api (quick) or spin up dedicated capacity or even private VPC for residency and compliance. Our security team also prefers keys in our KMS.
[01:20] Renee Cho: yep, SSO and audit logs are musts. SOC2 is table stakes for us. also, data at rest encryption and optional on-prem for later.
[01:30] Maya Chen: understood. quick question on traffic shape — is 100k requests/day fairly steady or spiky?
[01:36] Lena Ortiz: mostly steady but we get spikes during market open, 2-3x for about 30 minutes.
[01:42] Maya Chen: ok good to know. Diego, can you take latency vs cost framing and levers?
[01:48] Diego Alvarez: sure. first, per-token pricing is the main meter for hosted mode. you pay per token generated/consumed, and we surface sample unit costs for model choices. For dedicated, you buy reserved GPU capacity — predictable throughput and lower marginal per-token cost but with commit. For private, you get VPC/on-prem and full control, higher ops and license fees.
[02:08] Diego Alvarez: some concrete levers: batching (more efficient GPU utilization), prefix caching / KV cache (reuse decoder state for repeated prefixes), model quantization (reduced memory/throughput cost), and routing (send low-SLO requests to cheaper model variants).
[02:24] Samir Patel: can you quantify? we need to forecast whether 12k/mo covers 100k/day at our current prompt sizes.
[02:31] Diego Alvarez: high level ballpark: with hosted and a reasonably optimized medium-size open model, naive single-request serving might be, say, $0.0009 per input+output token combined — depends on model. But with batching + KV cache, you can often drop the effective per-token cost 20-40% depending on reuse and batch window. Dedicated can push per-token lower but requires a monthly commit — think of it as trading capex/commit for lower opex.
[02:58] Lena Ortiz: so for our numbers: 100k requests/day * ~210 tokens/request = 21M tokens/day, about 630M tokens/month. that seems high - if at $0.0009 per token we are blown way over budget.
[03:15] Diego Alvarez: good catch — that's why batching and cache are critical. if you can cache the prefix or use KV caching so only deltas are generated, your tokens/mth that incur full compute can be much lower. also, model choice matters — smaller model variants or trimmed output lengths reduce tokens.
[03:30] Tom Briggs: we do have a lot of repeated prefixes in the login prompts — same context, different user ids. Maybe KV cache will help.
[03:36] Maya Chen: also routing: high-risk flows could go to a higher-accuracy model, lower-risk to a cheaper one. that hybrid approach often meets SLA and budget.
[03:44] Renee Cho: but routing introduces complexity for compliance — if we route outside region for cheap model, residency issues pop up. we need region pinning.
[03:53] Diego Alvarez: yes, we support routing by policy (latency, cost, region). for residency you'd pin to region or private deployment.
[03:59] Samir Patel: what's the smallest pilot we can run to validate unit economics? we don't want to commit to dedicated without proof.
[04:06] Maya Chen: typical pilot is 2-3 weeks: we run your sample trace against hosted and a dedicated-mimic (we can run a reserved capacity simulation or a limited dedicated pool) and give you per-token bill and latency distribution. We'll also produce a batching/caching config to apply.
[04:20] Lena Ortiz: timeline wise we want results before Sept 15 — that's our budget review.
[04:24] Maya Chen: doable, we'll aim to ship pilot pricing and template in 48 hours.
[04:28] Diego Alvarez: technical note: for P99 100ms, that constraint is tough with larger models. If you need sub-200ms, we look at smaller models, aggressive batching windows, and colocated GPU pools. dedicated with GPU types tuned for inference (like A10x or H100 equivalents) helps. Also warm KV-cache reduces compute significantly for repeated interactions.
[04:50] Lena Ortiz: what's the realistic percent reduction from KV cache?
[04:53] Diego Alvarez: empirically we see 20-60% reduction in compute tokens for affinity-heavy workloads. if 70% of the prompt is static prefix you can save a lot. But it's workload dependent.
[05:04] Samir Patel: can you give a worked example for our numbers?
[05:07] Diego Alvarez: quick back-of-envelope: current raw tokens/month 630M. Assume KV cache reduces 50% of compute tokens (so billable compute tokens ~315M) and batching yields 25% throughput efficiency improvement translating to cost reduction on GPU time — it's not identical to token cost but effectively maybe another 15-25% on top. Combined you could potentially get ~55-60% effective cost reduction vs naive. So 630M * $0.0009 = $567k naive; with 60% reduction that's ~ $227k. Still >$12k budget, so more reductions needed: choose smaller model variants, trim outputs, or only run model on high-risk fraction.
[05:50] Tom Briggs: ok that math shows we need a heavy optimization: perhaps only 10% of auth flows go to model and the rest use heuristics.
[05:58] Lena Ortiz: yes we were planning that. our product asks for the model on high-confidence cases only, maybe 15% of traffic. That would change the tokens per month down to ~95M before other savings.
[06:12] Diego Alvarez: exactly. 95M tokens at $0.0009 naive would be $85k, with batching/cache and smaller models could be in the $20-30k band; dedicated might get you to $10-15k if traffic shape is steady and you commit. So that is where the decision boundary sits.
[06:29] Samir Patel: what does commit look like for dedicated — monthly seat or GPU pool?
[06:33] Diego Alvarez: it's a reserved GPU pool with monthly commit tiers. we can do shorter pilots with temporary dedicated pools or provide simulated pricing for the committed tiers. There's also burst capacity for spikes.
[06:43] Renee Cho: security: we need KMS integration so keys never leave our control, and audit logs for every model call. do you support Bring Your Own Key?
[06:51] Maya Chen: yes, for Private and Dedicated we support BYOK/KMS integration. Hosted supports customer-managed keys in certain enterprise plans. Audit logs and token-level traces are available in Console with retention options.
[07:02] Renee Cho: what about data residency? our legal says EU data can't leave EU.
[07:06] Diego Alvarez: we have region pinning for hosted, region-backed dedicated clusters, and fully private deployments for air-gapped or on-prem. We can pin model serving to an EU region.
[07:15] Lena Ortiz: performance testing — will you run our trace on your side?
[07:18] Diego Alvarez: yes, typical pilot: you provide obfuscated trace, we replay it against candidate models in hosted mode and a dedicated test pool to report latency P50/P95/P99 and cost breakdowns (tokens, GPU time, tail latency).
[07:31] Tom Briggs: and can you show expected reduction from batching windows? we want to understand impact on P99 because batching can increase tail sometimes.
[07:37] Diego Alvarez: correct — batching helps throughput but if you increase batch window you can increase latency variability. We tune to your SLO — e.g., a micro-batching window under 10ms can give some gains without hurting P99 much; continuous batching strategies can preserve P99 while increasing utilization. We'll propose initial configs and iterate.
[07:54] Samir Patel: any limitations around model variants? we use an open LLaMA derivative right now.
[07:59] Diego Alvarez: we support a range of open and proprietary models and can onboard custom weights. For private deployments you bring your model. For hosted, we curate models and can host specific open checkpoints on request after validation.
[08:11] Lena Ortiz: regarding latency numbers, what GPU types do you recommend for sub-150ms?
[08:16] Diego Alvarez: for the sequence lengths you described, an inference-optimized GPU (A100/H100-class) with optimized kernels or specialized inference hardware is best. We map kernel selection automatically. Dedicated pools let you pick target hardware.
[08:30] Marcus (finance): (quiet) what about pricing buckets — can you give a sample tier comparison?
[08:34] Maya Chen: sure, high level: hosted per-token bill; dedicated is monthly commit with lower per-token — we'll include concrete tier numbers in the pilot pricing sheet. Example: dedicated commit at mid-sized model usage can cut effective per-token 2-3x vs hosted. Private has platform fees plus lower per-token but higher ops cost.
[08:54] Renee Cho: also want to ask about SLA and fallbacks — if dedicated fails do you have transparent fallback to hosted?
[08:59] Diego Alvarez: yes, automatic fallback policies exist — we can route to hosted or a higher-latency lower-cost variant. Circuit-breakers and canary routing are supported.
[09:08] Tom Briggs: what success metrics should we agree on for the pilot?
[09:11] Maya Chen: suggested pilot success criteria: 1) demonstrate sustained P99 <= 150ms for targeted subset, 2) show >= 30% cost reduction via batching/caching for that subset OR bring per-month cost under $15k with defined routing fraction, 3) integration feasibility (KMS, audit logs) validated.
[09:30] Lena Ortiz: we can accept that, though the $15k target is aggressive.
[09:34] Marcus: finance will sign off only if we can show predictable capex.
[09:38] Maya Chen: understood. we'll include sensitivity scenarios in the report.
[09:42] (short pause, people typing)
[09:47] Diego Alvarez: quick note on measurement: we'll produce token-level cost breakout (input tokens, output tokens), GPU time, and an amortized per-request cost. We'll also show where batching/caching contributed.
[09:58] Samir Patel: can we instrument trace to see cache hit rates?
[10:01] Diego Alvarez: yes, our profiler surfaces cache hit rates and suggested cache TTLs.
[10:05] Lena Ortiz: what about function calling and structured outputs — does that change token accounting?
[10:10] Diego Alvarez: function calling reduces unstructured output length in many cases, but it can add tokens depending on serialization. It's a tradeoff; we'll account for it in the pilot.
[10:18] Renee Cho: ask: if we go private later, what is typical lead time?
[10:22] Maya Chen: private on-prem roster depends on infra — typical engagements are 6-12 weeks for a full private rollout, shorter for VPC deployments in cloud regions. We'll scope that if you want.
[10:31] Samir Patel: for the pilot, what access do we need to provide?
[10:34] Diego Alvarez: obfuscated logs/trace, a whitelist of endpoints, expected SLOs, and a contact for KMS questions. We'll provide a template for safe sharing.
[10:44] Lena Ortiz: ok we'll produce a sanitized sample of 7 days.
[10:48] Maya Chen: perfect. two quick clarifying questions: 1) do you expect to limit model usage to a subset of traffic (you said 10-15%)? 2) is the $12k/month hard cap for the quarter?
[10:58] Lena Ortiz: yes on subset — we plan ~15% initially. $12k is the working constraint but we can stretch a little with exec sign-off if pilot looks promising.
[11:08] Maya Chen: great. we'll propose scenarios for 10%, 15%, 25% routing fractions so you can see sensitivity.
[11:15] Tom Briggs: what about observability — token-level cost per endpoint?
[11:18] Diego Alvarez: Console has per-route and per-model dashboards, token breakdowns, and traces. We can grant a sandbox project for you to explore.
[11:26] Renee Cho: final security shout: will the audit logs include redacted prompt text? we need to preserve PII constraints.
[11:33] Maya Chen: yes — we can redact or exclude prompt text from logs, and keep metadata for troubleshooting. That will be part of the pilot contract.
[11:41] (some chatter about scheduling)
[11:45] Maya Chen: recap and next steps: 1) Maya sends pilot pricing and template by 2026-08-24, 2) Lena uploads obfuscated 7-day trace by 2026-08-25, 3) Diego and Samir schedule a 60-minute technical kickoff next week to configure batching and cache, 4) Redwood runs trace and returns cost/latency report by Sept 10.
[12:05] Lena Ortiz: agreed.
[12:09] Marcus: finance side: please include a best/worst case in the costing, we'll want to see committed dedicated vs hosted delta.
[12:15] Maya Chen: will do. any final questions?
[12:19] Tom Briggs: not from product.
[12:21] Renee Cho: not from security. thanks.
[12:23] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links.
[12:26] (call ends)

Notes: transcription contains occasional misattributions and minor mis-hearings. Some model and GPU type names were abbreviated in conversation.
